text: Section 46.41 ). H93   1260 – 1368, Yüan dynasty   Chen Chuan Chi and others described honey collection, presumably from A. dorsata. K68 Li Ji wrote Yulizi, lingqui zhagren , describing beekeeping through the seasons, including the uniting and dividing of colonies, and control of enemies. C93 1271 The Yüan emperor established a Board of Agriculture. N84 1273 The above Board printed Nung snag chi yao [Fundamentals of agriculture and sericulture], which included beekeeping. It was immediately distributed all over the country (then the northern provinces and Szechwan), but no copy survives. N84   1368 – 1644, Ming dynasty   1490-1570 Li Su Tren wrote Ben cau Kang mu , saying ‘Honey is made tightly, therefore called honey’. KYF 1553 Wang Shi-Chin completed Chi-pei-yau-tan , which referred to the families of Yau-yue who regarded a day on which their bees swarmed as unfailingly lucky, so they regulated their lives by observing their hives. R37 1596 In Pên Tschao Kang Mu [Great pharmacopaeia], Li Shih Chen tried to explain the origin of the word for honey. APPENDIX 2 Some Beekeeping Museums This Appendix gives names and addresses of some beekeeping museums, and general museums with material on the history of beekeeping. Entries marked* were confirmed in 1996. Earlier lists have been issued (Crane, 1979, 1983a, 1990a), and a detailed guide is being published by Apimondia, IITEA, Bd Ficusului 42, Bucharest 71544, Romania. Museums listed differ greatly in the number of historical items held, and in the proportion of beekeeping material on public display. They also vary in their days and hours of opening, and material in certain museums can be seen only by appointment. The list does not include exhibitions on modern beekeeping or the life of bees.
